intro: Yellowstone is the oldest national park in the United States, high on the plateau of northwest Wyoming. Its one tree on our map is not alive: the Petrified Tree near Tower Junction, a redwood trunk turned to stone, buried by volcanic deposits 45 to 50 million years ago and still standing upright behind an iron fence. A reader sent us its photograph.
meta_description: The Petrified Tree near Tower Junction in Yellowstone: a redwood trunk turned to stone 45 to 50 million years ago, where it stands and how to see it.
question_meta: The Petrified Tree near Tower Junction in Yellowstone: a redwood trunk turned to stone 45 to 50 million years ago, where it stands and how to see it.
question_answer: The Petrified Tree stands just west of Tower Junction in the northeast of Yellowstone National Park, a short walk from a small parking area off the Grand Loop Road. It is a fossil, the trunk of an ancient redwood, not a living tree, and it stands behind an iron fence. The park's entrance fee applies.
question_context: The Petrified Tree is the stone trunk of a redwood that grew in Yellowstone long before the park's present forests of pine and fir. The National Park Service calls it an excellent example of an ancient redwood and dates the burial of these forests to 45 to 50 million years ago, when volcanic deposits and mudflows covered them quickly enough to stop the wood from rotting. A reader who stood beside it sent us the photograph on this page, with a GPS fix that places our pin. It shows a pale trunk, cream and grey with streaks of rust, taller than the iron fence that surrounds it, the old grain of the wood still visible in the cracks and splinters of the stone, and the top broken off jagged. Travel guides say the fence keeps souvenir hunters away. It stands near the Lost Lake trailhead, west of Tower Junction, on the road between Mammoth and the Lamar Valley, so it is an easy stop on a drive through the northeast of the park. The park entrance fee applies, and the walk from the parking area is short.

faq.q: Is the Petrified Tree in Yellowstone a living tree?
faq.a: No. It is the trunk of an ancient redwood turned to stone. The National Park Service dates the burial of these forests by volcanic deposits and mudflows to 45 to 50 million years ago.
Just west of Tower Junction in the northeast of the park, near the Lost Lake trailhead, a short walk from a small parking area off the Grand Loop Road.

faq.q: Why is the Petrified Tree fenced?
faq.a: To protect it. Travel guides say souvenir hunters damaged the petrified trees that once stood near it, and an iron fence now surrounds the one that remains.

trees.story:
This is not a living tree, and it has not been one for tens of millions of years. The Petrified Tree, west of Tower Junction in Yellowstone, is the trunk of a redwood turned to stone, which the National Park Service calls an excellent example of an ancient redwood. The park explains how it lasted: volcanic deposits and mudflows buried the forests here 45 to 50 million years ago, quickly enough to keep the wood from rotting.

A reader sent us this photograph with a GPS fix taken beside it, and stone or not, it still reads as a tree. The trunk stands taller than the iron fence around it, pale cream and grey with streaks of rust, its surface cracked into blocks and splinters along the old grain, its top snapped off jagged against the sky. Travel guides say the fence is there to keep souvenir hunters away from it.

The reader gives it as a redwood, fifty million years old, and the park's account agrees with them.

Come on a clear afternoon and walk along the fence, so that you see the grain from more than one side.
